name: Desiccated beef testicle supplements

card.summary: Dried bovine testicle capsules sold on a 'like supports like' basis; the idea descends from 1889 organ-extract experiments later attributed to placebo.
card.note: One registered trial of an organ-supplement product on testosterone is listed as active; no results found.

quick.overview:
These are capsules or powders made from dried beef testicle, sold as a way to support male hormones on the principle that eating an organ supports the same organ in the body. They belong to the older tradition of organotherapy.

No published trial results were found. A trial of a product described as an organ-based supplement, with testosterone as its condition, is registered as active but not recruiting.
quick.mechanism: Proponents propose that nutrients or hormone-related compounds in the organ support the corresponding function in the eater. Historians note that Brown-Sequard's 1889 testicular extracts did not yield active amounts of testosterone and that the reported effects are now thought to reflect placebo [1].
quick.risks: The sources reviewed do not describe safety data for these products. Wikipedia notes that many historical glandular extracts were promoted without systematic evidence of safety and efficacy [2].

lead: Desiccated beef testicle supplements are dried, usually encapsulated, preparations of bovine testicular tissue sold as dietary supplements. They are promoted within the 'like supports like' idea that consuming an organ benefits the same organ in the consumer.

The idea has a long lineage. Organotherapy used animal glands and tissues as treatments and contributed to modern endocrinology, although many preparations were ineffective, poorly standardised or promoted without systematic evidence [2]. In 1889 the physiologist Charles-Edouard Brown-Sequard reported injecting himself with testicular extract; his claims were dismissed by contemporaries, and the positive responses are now thought to have been placebo [1].
No completed clinical trials of the oral supplements were found.

paras: Organotherapy, also called opotherapy, aimed to replace absent or insufficient internal secretions with organ preparations [2]. In 1889, at age 72, Brown-Sequard told the Societe de Biologie in Paris that injections of testicular fluid from guinea pigs and dogs rejuvenated him, and thousands of men tried the therapy [1]. Endocrinologist Robert Greenblatt argued that it could not have worked, because the testes do not store their hormones, and later experiments found that the method did not yield active amounts of testosterone [1]. Standardised hormone treatments largely replaced crude organ preparations [2].

No studies found with published results. A registered study, NCT07256639, evaluates a company's whole-food organ supplement package on men's health with testosterone as the listed condition; it enrolled 100 participants, started in October 2025 and is listed as active, not recruiting [3].
Organ-meat and glandular supplements are marketed in ancestral-diet and testosterone-focused communities. No community sources were available to quote for this article.

timeline.event: Brown-Sequard reports self-injection of animal testicular extract in Paris; the claims are dismissed by contemporaries [1].
George Redmayne Murray treats myxoedema with sheep-thyroid extract, spurring interest in other organ extracts [2].
